html:
"England and Ireland" is the map's label for the lands of the English crown from 1530 to 1700: England with Wales, and Ireland. Scotland is drawn separately, since it kept its own crown and parliament until 1707.

Henry VIII broke with Rome in the Act of Supremacy of 1534, and in 1542 he made himself King of Ireland instead of its lord. For the next century the English crown fought to make that title real:

  • Under Elizabeth I the Nine Years' War broke the last great Gaelic lords by 1603.
  • The Plantation of Ulster from 1609 settled English and Scottish Protestants on confiscated land.
  • In 1603 James VI of Scotland inherited England in the Union of the Crowns, so one king ruled three kingdoms.

Civil wars across all three kingdoms in the 1640s ended with Oliver Cromwell's brutal conquest of Ireland in 1649. The Catholic King James II lost his throne in 1688 and was beaten in Ireland at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. England joined Scotland in 1707, and Ireland stayed a separate Kingdom of Ireland.
sum: "England and Ireland" is the map's label for the lands of the English crown from 1530 to 1700: England with Wales, and Ireland. Scotland is drawn separately, since it kept its own crown and parliament until 1707.
